paras: The lynching of Charlie Burwell was the hanging of an elderly Black man near Meridian, Mississippi, on a Saturday night in late July 1895. Early reports said he was killed on suspicion of a July 4 assault on a storekeeping couple, but later accounts said the real assailants killed him because he had been promised a reward to find them. The story ran as a wire dispatch or one-line brief in papers across the country and in Mississippi state columns.

On the night of July 4, Lewis Farmer and his wife, who ran a small store about two miles from Meridian, were "murderously assaulted and left for dead," and their store was robbed. The assailants escaped, and by early August several suspects were held in jail. According to a Mississippi column, hold-ups and attempted murders in the area had "stirred the people to fever heat."

Burwell, described as "colored" and about 65 years old, lived within a stone's throw of the Farmer store. Dispatches dated July 28 and 29 placed the lynching on Saturday night, while one copy dated July 30 said "last night." According to the Mississippi account, his killers went to his house, dragged him to Sowashee bridge and "strung him from a beam."

The first explanation was that Burwell had been "concerned in the Farmer outrage." The same dispatch added that "later developments" pointed to the real culprits, since Burwell had been promised a $250 reward to "ferret out the guilty parties" and they learned of it. Other briefs said he had evidence that would implicate the Farmer assailants and was about to betray them.
No report of an inquest, an arrest of the lynchers or any official response appears in the coverage.

The Meridian dispatch reached white papers from Ohio to Idaho within a week, often under heads such as "An Old Negro Lynched" and "A Mississippi Lynching." The headlines split along the two explanations: the Stark County Democrat's read "Persons Guilty of a Crime Hang Him to Keep Him Quiet," while the Kootenai Herald's read "A Mississippi Mob Thought He Murdered the Farmers." Condensed news columns in Wisconsin, North Dakota and Kansas reduced it to a sentence, some saying "a mob" acted and some calling the Farmer crime "a recent double murder."

In Mississippi, the Oxford Eagle and the Grenada Sentinel ran a longer piece, "A Lynching at Meridian," which supplied the bridge and the jailed suspects and offered no comment on the killing. No Black-press coverage of the lynching was found.

Accounts disagree on who killed Burwell and why: briefs credited a mob that thought him guilty of the Farmer crime, while the fuller texts favored the "later developments" that the assailants silenced him. Neither version names a source, and no report gives the number of men involved.

reader.title: Lynching of Charlie Burwell
bases: Every report calls the hanging of Burwell near Meridian a lynching, and briefs attribute it to 'a mob' (A1, A4, A12, A18).

Burwell was hanged by private persons with no lawful authority (A1, A18); briefs call them 'a mob' but give no number (A4, A12). The first reports say he was thought concerned in the Farmer assault, a justice pretext, but later versions say the actual assailants killed him to stop him betraying them (A1, A5, A18), so the pretext is uncertain.
The Meridian wire dispatch (A1, A6, A12) and a separately written Mississippi column with added local details (A18, A19) agree that Burwell, about 65, was hanged near Meridian in late July.

framing.detail: Northern and western papers ran the dispatch or a one-line brief under heads such as 'An Old Negro Lynched' and 'A Mississippi Lynching', calling Burwell 'colored' or 'an aged negro'.
Headlines split between the suspicion story ('A Mississippi Mob Thought He Murdered the Farmers') and the silencing story ('Persons Guilty of a Crime Hang Him to Keep Him Quiet').
Mississippi papers ran 'A Lynching at Meridian' without comment, placing it amid hold-ups that had 'stirred the people to fever heat'.
